extracted.intended_audience: psychologists and psychometricians studying humour/temperament and cross-cultural instrument validation
extracted.subtask_description: Cross-national psychometric validation of the State-Trait Cheerfulness Inventory (trait, 60-item version) in a Chinese sample, testing factor structure, measurement invariance, and associations with personality, humour styles, and well‑being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-dimensional factor structure (cheerfulness, seriousness, bad mood)
rubrics_metrics.description: The STCI-T60 consists of three dimensions of cheerfulness, seriousness, and bad mood integrated to measure the temperamental basis of the sense of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate that the instrument separates into these three latent factors (cheerfulness, seriousness, bad mood); use the 60-item standard trait version consistent with other language versions when testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication of factor structure across cultures
rubrics_metrics.description: The present study replicated the three-dimensional factor structure of the STCI in China using 60 items consistent with other standard trait versions (e.g., English, Chilean-Spanish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confirmatory factor analysis to test whether the same factor structure found in other language versions holds in the target cultural sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement invariance (multi-group CFA: configural/metric/structural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using multi-group confirmatory factor analyses, partial metric invariance was found between English and Chinese versions of the STCI-T60, but structural invariance was not observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test successive levels of invariance (configural, metric, scalar, structural) across language/cultural groups; partial metric invariance may be acceptable, but lack of structural invariance indicates differences in latent structure and requires cautious interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent and criterion validity with personality, humour styles, and well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations between the STCI traits and major personality dimensions, humour styles, and well-being were examined; cheerfulness and seriousness showed positive associations with satisfaction with life and emotional well-being (EWB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess correlations and regression relationships between STCI scales and external constructs (big five/personality measures, humour styles inventories, life satisfaction, EWB) to establish convergent and criterion validity and expected directional patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model and test non-linear (curvilinear) trait associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Closer examination suggested bad mood showed curvilinear associations with both cheerfulness and seriousness, such that cheerfulness and bad mood were negatively associated for those low and average in trait bad mood but not for those with high trait bad mood; seriousness was positively associated with bad mood at high levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume strictly linear relationships among trait scales—model quadratic or other non-linear terms (e.g., piecewise, interaction) when examining inter-trait associations and their links to outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item and version consistency with standard trait forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The study used 60 items consistent with other standard trait versions (e.g., English, Chilean-Spanish).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conducting cross-national validation, use item sets aligned with established standard versions to facilitate comparisons and invariance testing; document any item modifications or translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multi-group confirmatory factor analysis as primary method
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-group confirmatory factor analyses were used to assess cross-national invariance between English and Chinese versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ MGCFA procedures (appropriate model fit indices, nested model comparisons) to evaluate equivalence across groups rather than relying solely on exploratory methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation within cultural frameworks (e.g., dialecticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implications based on the empirical literature in dialecticism and cross-cultural assessment were discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret validation results in light of cultural theories (such as dialectical thinking) that may explain differences in factor structure or trait associations across cultures; consider cultural context when drawing conclusions about construct meaning.
